findings.text: Waiter records hold bucket linkage plus a private wait queue plus a token plus a creator processor identifier plus a flag separating real sleepers from placeholders for early wakes. Buckets pair a guard with a chain head and form a fixed table indexed by token hash.
Sleep table addressing uses eight hash bits and two hundred fifty six buckets.
Paravirtual interrupt fanout groups destination identifiers into windows sized at twice the native word width.

Each sleep bucket has its own guard that protects lookup insertion and removal. Hold time covers only list mutation. The blocking wait path requires disabled interrupts on entry and reenables them while descheduled. Placeholder allocation happens outside the guard.
Bucket search matches tokens by equality. Insertion reports failure when the token already exists, consuming and freeing a placeholder entry when present so the later waiter does not block.

A waiter that successfully enqueues sleeps exclusively and uninterruptibly until its record leaves the table, then completes its wait. A prior wake that left a placeholder suppresses sleeping entirely.

Waking uses a reserved all ones token to release every local processor entry across all buckets. Other tokens wake one matching entry when present and otherwise leave a placeholder so a future waiter returns immediately.

If placeholder storage cannot be allocated the waker yields the processor briefly and rechecks for completion before retrying, avoiding duplicate entries. Storage allocated but ultimately unneeded is released.
A helper exposes current processor async fault state, returning no flags when the mechanism is disabled and otherwise returning pending reason bits while clearing stored state.

The async fault entry returns without action when no reason is pending. When pending it validates trap context and either waits for the associated token on swapped out pages or logs unexpected reasons, always pairing entry and exit handling.
Faults observed with interrupts disabled in the saved trap state are treated as fatal host errors, as are swapped out faults observed in privileged mode.

The hypervisor callback vector acknowledges the local interrupt controller and accounts the event, then when enabled wakes the stored token, clears token storage and acknowledges completion to the host.

Guest end of interrupt first attempts to clear a per processor indicator and skip the native action on success, falling back to the native action otherwise. Correctness relies on host access occurring only on the owning processor.
Steal time is sampled with a versioned sequence and ordering barriers, discarding samples taken during an update as indicated by an odd or changing version and returning only a stable counter.

Processor setup conditionally enables async fault delivery as an interrupt with optional exit based delivery, enables paravirtual end of interrupt with an aligned shared indicator, and registers steal time storage. Teardown clears each control that was enabled.

Online brings up guest state with interrupts held. Offline tears down steal, end of interrupt, migration and fault controls and releases local waiters except during shutdown, plus disables the guest clock. Suspend and resume, reboot notification and crash paths reuse offline and online helpers.
On encrypted confidential guests the shared per processor fault, steal and interrupt indicator pages are mapped without encryption before their addresses are shared with the host.

Paravirtual fanout ignores empty sets, distinguishes normal vectors from nonmaskable delivery, packs nearby destination identifiers into one host call and starts a new call when an identifier falls outside the current window. A variant excludes the caller via per processor scratch storage.

Paravirtual remote flush, interrupt fanout and scheduling yield are each enabled only when required host features are present and configuration excludes realtime hints, single processor systems and platforms with native waiting support where applicable.

Remote flush avoids disturbing preempted processors by marking them for deferred flush with an atomic update and removing them from the immediate set, then flushing only the remaining online set natively while preventing preemption.
Call function delivery first uses the native mechanism and then offers at most one scheduling yield to a non idle preempted destination.

Availability reports whether a cached hypervisor interface base is nonzero. The base is discovered once using processor level, hypervisor presence and signature matching. Feature and hint queries derive from that base.

Early initialization establishes paravirtual identity, reboot handling, sleep bucket guards, steal and preemption callbacks, interrupt callbacks, async fault vectoring, remote flush and yield overrides, boot and hotplug hooks, crash handling, power management hooks and lockup detector policy.

Paravirtual spinlocks stay disabled for realtime hints, single processor systems, explicit opt out, or missing host halt support. Otherwise lock hashing and slow path plus unlock plus wait plus kick overrides are installed and the generic virt key is turned off.

Preemption state is queryable from a per processor steal record flag, with both a portable accessor and an assembly sequence. Guest clock teardown clears the system time control when one is configured.

Migration readiness is programmed only when the guest is encrypted and capable plus firmware boot and runtime services exist and a firmware variable explicitly enables live migration. Missing variables, access failures and disabled values leave the control untouched.
A global blocking helper waits for completion of a prior async fault identified by token and returns immediately when completion was already recorded.
Spinlock setup is exposed as an early global initialization entry that selects between paravirtual and native locking based on host and command line policy.
Two internal flags record whether steal time support was negotiated and whether guest polling was active across suspend.
Power management linkage pairs suspend and resume callbacks in an operations record referenced by a registered core object.
Interrupt and flush helpers use per processor scratch mask storage to avoid allocation in atomic context.
